lesson.title: When the Safe Base Isn't So Safe
lesson.summary: Insecure attachment describes patterns in which infants show difficulty using their caregiver as a reliable source of comfort, including avoidant and anxious/ambivalent styles identified through the Strange Situation.
lesson.body:
Not every infant in Ainsworth's Strange Situation shows the secure pattern of easy comfort-seeking and quick soothing at reunion. Insecure attachment is the general term for the patterns in which an infant's relationship with their caregiver does not function smoothly as a reliable secure base, and Ainsworth's original research identified two main insecure patterns, with later researchers identifying additional categories still.

In the avoidant pattern, infants show little distress when the caregiver leaves and, notably, tend to avoid or ignore the caregiver at reunion, rather than seeking them out for comfort, sometimes appearing more focused on toys than on the returning caregiver. This pattern has often been associated with caregiving that is consistently unresponsive or that discourages the expression of distress, though it is worth being cautious about assuming a single simple cause, since researchers have also debated how much of this pattern reflects the infant's temperament interacting with the caregiving environment rather than caregiving alone.

In the anxious, or resistant, pattern, sometimes called anxious-ambivalent, infants tend to be highly distressed by the separation and then show a mixed, hard-to-soothe reaction at reunion, seeking closeness with the caregiver while simultaneously resisting or pushing away the comfort being offered, sometimes appearing angry or clingy at once. This pattern is often associated with caregiving that has been inconsistent, sometimes responsive and sometimes not, which researchers suggest may leave the infant uncertain whether comfort will actually be available, producing this push-pull response.

Later researchers, including Mary Main, identified a further category sometimes called disorganized attachment, in which the infant's behavior at reunion lacks a clear, coherent strategy altogether, sometimes appearing confused, frozen, or contradictory, a pattern that has been studied in connection with more disrupted or frightening caregiving environments. As with secure attachment, it is important not to overstate what any single insecure classification means for a child's future. Insecure attachment patterns are associated with somewhat higher average rates of later social and emotional difficulties in large-scale research, but these are statistical tendencies observed across groups, not individual predictions, and attachment patterns can also shift over time as a child's relationships and environment change. Attachment theory offers a genuinely useful early window into a child's relational world, not a permanent label.
